title: Global regularity or breakdown of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations

concept.text: A proof that smooth, globally defined solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations exist in three dimensions for smooth initial data, or an example where they break down, as posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute. Sources given: https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/ ; https://world-of-mathematics.com/blog/millennium-problems-overview/.

page.title: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness
page.definition: A proof settles whether three-dimensional incompressible viscous flow with no external force stays smooth for all time from every smooth initial velocity, or can blow up in finite time. Smooth velocity and pressure have derivatives of every order; incompressibility means zero velocity divergence; at a blow-up time the velocity becomes unbounded.

goal.need: These equations describe incompressible viscous fluid motion. Global smoothness is proved in 2 dimensions. Clay’s 3-dimensional formulation asks for one of 4 proofs: global smoothness with zero force (A, B), or breakdown for some smooth initial velocity and smooth force (C, D). Its description also states the dichotomy without force: either A and B hold, or some smooth initial velocity has a solution with a finite blowup time. This page tests that unforced question. Clay assigns $1 million to resolution.

completion.title: Clay confirms a proof of global smoothness, or of finite-time blow-up with zero force.
completion.criterion: CMI determines under §7 of its prize rules that a complete proof settles the regularity question with zero force, for ν>0: global C∞ velocity and pressure for every admissible smooth divergence-free initial velocity with f=0, on R³ (A) or R³/Z³ (B); or one such initial velocity with f=0 whose smooth solution blows up in finite time, on R³ with bounded energy or on R³/Z³. Breakdown that needs a nonzero force does not meet this test. Before CMI rules, a proof counts as a claim only if a proof assistant checks the whole result; a proof that rests on unreleased data, or on computation outside the proof assistant, does not.
completion.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute: Fefferman’s official problem description and §§4–7 of the Millennium Prize Description and Rules adopted on 26 September 2018. The Atlas restricts Clay’s breakdown alternatives C and D to zero force, following the dichotomy that Fefferman’s description states.
completion.threshold_quote: Either (A) and (B) hold, or else there is a smooth, divergence-free u◦(x) for which (1), (2), (3) have a solution with a finite blowup time.
completion.basis: Clay’s prize statement also accepts breakdown with a nonzero force (C or D). This page does not: Fefferman’s description puts the regularity question at zero force, and forced breakdown is a separate milestone here. Clay’s announcement of 11 September 2026 acknowledged an apparent solution and kept its evaluation procedure. Alpöge and Buckmaster’s paper of 20 November 2026 claims blow-up with zero force; its certificate is not released, and the check that the certificate satisfies the conditions is outside its Lean formalization.

milestones.title: Every admissible smooth initial velocity has a smooth Navier–Stokes solution for some T > 0.
milestones.criterion: For ν>0 and f=0, each admissible smooth divergence-free initial velocity has smooth velocity and pressure on 0≤t<T for some T>0 depending on the initial velocity. Leray proved whole-space local existence in 1934; Clay’s description records local existence for both domains.
milestones.set_by: The field’s local-existence theorem, established for whole space by Leray and recognized for both domains in Clay’s official problem description.
milestones.threshold_quote: small time interval [0, T), with T depending on the initial data.

milestones.title: Every finite-energy divergence-free initial velocity has a global Leray–Hopf weak solution.
milestones.criterion: For ν>0 and f=0, every divergence-free u₀∈L² has a solution for all t≥0, satisfying the equations against smooth test functions and attaining u₀ strongly in L² at t=0. For each finite T, u∈L∞(0,T;L²) and ∇u∈L²(0,T;L²), with ½||u(t)||₂²+ν∫₀ᵗ||∇u(s)||₂²ds≤½||u₀||₂². Leray proved whole-space existence in 1934; the cited 2021 proof treats both domains. Smoothness is not asserted.
milestones.set_by: Leray–Hopf existence theory; Definitions 1–2 and the existence theorems in Berselli and Spirito’s published treatment specify the weak-solution and energy conditions.
milestones.threshold_quote: There exists a Leray-Hopf weak solution u

milestones.title: Suitable weak Navier–Stokes solutions have zero one-dimensional parabolic singular-set measure.
milestones.criterion: For ν>0 and f=0, a suitable weak solution, which also obeys the local energy inequality, has a singular set S with P₁(S)=0. P₁ is the one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure, using cylinders with spatial radius r and time length r². This permits isolated singular points. Caffarelli, Kohn and Nirenberg proved this partial-regularity result in 1982. Its local conclusion applies in whole space and on the periodic domain.
milestones.set_by: The Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg theorem, stated in Clay’s official description and recognized by the American Mathematical Society’s 2014 Steele Prize.
milestones.threshold_quote: Let E be the singular set of u. Then P1(E) = 0.

milestones.title: The mathematics community generally accepts a proof of one Clay Navier–Stokes alternative.
milestones.criterion: For the domain being tracked, a complete proof of its global-smoothness or breakdown alternative achieves general acceptance in the global mathematics community, as determined by CMI under §7(a)(i). OpenAI’s 2026 preprint claims breakdown on both domains with smooth forcing of compact time support and zero initial velocity; it is not peer reviewed. An unreviewed preprint submitted on 6 October 2026 reports mismatches between the prose and Lean proofs. The cited documents do not establish that this acceptance threshold has been met.
milestones.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, §7(a)(i) of the Millennium Prize Description and Rules; this is the first evaluation stage before Clay’s detailed examination.
milestones.threshold_quote: First, a Proposed Solution must achieve general acceptance in the global mathematics community

milestones.title: Breakdown is proved for some smooth initial velocity and smooth force (Clay’s alternative C or D).
milestones.criterion: For ν>0, a complete proof exhibits a smooth divergence-free initial velocity and a smooth force, under Clay’s decay conditions on R³ (C) or periodicity conditions on R³/Z³ (D), for which no smooth solution exists for all time; on R³ the solution must also have bounded energy. The force may be nonzero and the initial velocity may be zero. The proof is public in full, as a written proof or as one checked in a proof assistant. General acceptance and a CMI ruling are not required. Clay’s prize statement accepts this alternative; this page’s completion test does not.
milestones.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, statements (C) and (D) of Fefferman’s official problem description.
milestones.threshold_quote: (C) Breakdown of Navier–Stokes solutions on R3.

milestones.title: A proof settling the unforced question is published in a refereed outlet meeting Clay’s conditions.
milestones.criterion: A complete proof of global smoothness with f=0 (A or B), or of finite-time blow-up of a smooth solution with f=0, on R³ with bounded energy or on R³/Z³, is published by a Qualifying Outlet under §6 of Clay’s rules: a refereed mathematics publication of worldwide repute with a named editorial board, a published refereeing process and a listing in MathSciNet, or a publication CMI approves under relaxed conditions. A preprint, a repository or an announcement is not such a publication. Clay’s 2 years of examination begin at this publication.
milestones.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, §§4(a) and 6 of the Millennium Prize Description and Rules; the restriction to zero force is this page’s.
milestones.threshold_quote: the Proposed Solution has been published by a Qualifying Outlet
